channel.title: Philippine Trade News, Russia–Philippines Trade Link
channel.description: Short notes on Philippine imports, tariffs, prices and demand, with a link to the original publication. Collected twice a week.

item.title: Issue of 12 November 2026
item.description:
What this means. This batch is mixed, but the pork story matters most: the Philippines has temporarily stopped imports of pork and offal, and industry groups want the ban extended with higher duties restored, so pork shipments over the coming months should wait. Check whether your product codes fall under the order and do not ship until your importer or the agriculture department confirms in writing. Vegetable suppliers face similar pressure from farm groups, and importers are also pushing back on inflated carrier charges at Philippine ports, so recalculate landed cost before quoting.

item.title: Issue of 9 November 2026
item.description:
What this means. The only direct opening for a Russian supplier here is the medical platform: the trade mission's stand is meant to run as a permanent exhibition, and proposals go to the listed address, so it is worth sending one now while participation is still small. The rest are tightening signals. The pork ban is justified by protecting local producers, so check the same risk for any category where the Philippines has domestic output. Customs wants deconsolidators to post a deposit and is collecting record revenue while import volumes fall, which means closer inspection, valuation scrutiny and tougher demands on intermediaries. Confirm who deconsolidates your shipments and whether they can meet the new terms, and keep small orders off consolidated parcel channels.

item.title: Issue of 2 November 2026
item.description:
What this means. The peso's slide makes all imports more expensive, so Russian fertilizer and rice suppliers should renegotiate price and payment currency with Filipino partners now instead of assuming last season's terms. Customs is simplifying procedures with authorized economic operator status and port recognition of export-oriented enterprise certificates with VAT exemption, which is worth checking against your specific importer. Holiday demand keeps poultry imports flowing and a business group wants the swine sector reviewed before any measures, so watch for possible pork restrictions, while the dairy, electronics export and nuclear items barely touch Russian supply.

item.title: Issue of 26 October 2026
item.description:
What this means. The thing to watch in the coming weeks is pork: the agriculture ministry wants a sharp tariff increase and is discussing a pause in issuing SPSIC from mid November to January. If the pause happens, check whether your shipments can secure permits before then and avoid locking current tariff rates into contracts. Russian meat suppliers should hold off on new shipments until the decision is clear, especially since Colombia has just been approved as a supplier, while the November trade commission in Manila on a possible free trade zone and the Supreme Court ruling on royalties in customs value are worth noting for fruit and import payment planning.

item.title: Issue of 22 October 2026
item.description:
What this means. The pork file is the one to watch: Manila is weighing a pause on import clearances, running a safeguard investigation and reviewing tariffs, while quota applications for next year are already open. Suppliers should first confirm with their Philippine buyer that a clearance is already issued before booking any shipment. The other items are scattered and the port congestion order is not in force yet, so build extra lead time into delivery plans and follow the tariff decisions expected in late October.

item.title: Issue of 19 October 2026
item.description:
What this means. The items in this digest are scattered, but on pork they point the same way: duties are set to rise while existing stocks will already hold back buying for the coming months and into next year. Pork suppliers should confirm the rate and the timing with local importers before committing shipments. For perishables, the more relevant move is to check which partners will get the new cold storage capacity and on what terms they accept cargo. Rice purchases are rising on weather risk and mostly concern Asian suppliers, while the overall backdrop is that food prices remain the main concern for buyers, so price is the first thing an importer will ask about.
